segments.text: We arrive holding two pieces from before: Rutherford's tiny nucleus, and Planck and Einstein's world of discrete quanta. Bohr's genius was to weld them together.

But first, the crisis. Rutherford's revolving electron is an accelerating charge, and classical physics insists such a charge must continuously radiate energy, spiral inward, and crash in about ten to the minus eight seconds.
Atoms plainly do not collapse in a flash, so something in the classical picture is missing.

The clue that cracked it open is the hydrogen line spectrum. Split hydrogen's glow with a prism and you get a handful of sharp separate coloured lines, with darkness in between $-$ not a smooth rainbow.
Here is the analogy that makes it click: compare a wheelchair ramp with a staircase.
On a ramp you can stop at any height, which is continuous, like classical physics. On a staircase you can only stand on step one, step two, step three $-$ never halfway.
The sharp lines are telling us the electron lives on a staircase of allowed energies, not on a ramp.
When the electron drops from a higher step to a lower one, it releases the exact energy difference as a single photon. Because only certain steps exist, only certain colours appear.
Hum do pieces lekar aaye hain: Rutherford ka tiny nucleus, aur Planck-Einstein ki discrete quanta wali duniya. Bohr ki genius thi in dono ko weld karna.

Par pehle crisis. Rutherford ka revolving electron ek accelerating charge hai, aur classical physics kehti hai ki aisa charge continuously energy radiate karega, andar spiral karega, aur lagbhag ten to the minus eight seconds mein crash ho jaayega.
Atoms clearly ek pal mein collapse नहीं hote, toh classical picture mein kuch missing hai.
Jo clue ise khol deta hai wo hai hydrogen line spectrum. Hydrogen ki glow ko prism se todo toh kuch sharp alag coloured lines milti hain, beech mein andhera $-$ smooth rainbow नहीं.
Ye rahी wo analogy jo baat samjha deti hai: wheelchair ramp ki tulna staircase se karo.
Ramp par aap kisi bhi height par ruk sakte ho, jo continuous hai, classical physics ki tarah. Staircase par aap sirf step one, step two, step three par khade ho sakte ho $-$ kabhi beech mein नहीं.
Sharp lines humein bata rahी hain ki electron allowed energies ki staircase par rehta hai, ramp par नहीं.
Jab electron ऊpar wale step se neeche wale par girta hai, wo exact energy difference ek single photon ke roop mein chhodta hai. Kyunki sirf kuch steps hain, sirf kuch colours aate hain.

sections.title: Bohr's bold rules and a preview of what breaks them

board_events.text: Bohr welds nucleus and quanta together (1913)
Electrons orbit only in certain stationary orbits where, against classical expectation, they do NOT radiate.
Each orbit has a fixed radius and a fixed energy; radiation happens only on a jump between orbits.
$m v r = \dfrac{n h}{2\pi}$: the integer $n$ (principal quantum number) labels the staircase steps.
This nailed hydrogen's exact line wavelengths $-$ a spectacular success.
But it is a brilliant patch: de Broglie (1924) gives the electron a wave nature; Heisenberg (1927) forbids a simultaneous exact position and momentum.
Bohr works only for one-electron species: H, He$^+$, Li$^{2+}$, Be$^{3+}$.
For a cricket ball the wave nature is unobservably tiny $-$ which is why the everyday world looks classical.

segments.text: Niels Bohr, in nineteen thirteen, turned the staircase picture into a model with a few bold rules.
He declared that an electron orbits the nucleus only in certain stationary orbits where, against all classical expectation, it simply does not radiate energy.
Each such orbit carries a fixed radius and a fixed energy, and the electron radiates only when it jumps between orbits.
To pin down which orbits are allowed, Bohr added a quantisation rule: the angular momentum can only be a whole-number multiple of h over two pi, and that integer n labels the steps.
This worked spectacularly. It predicted the exact wavelengths of every hydrogen spectral line, which is a stunning thing for a model to do.
But it was a brilliant patch, not a final theory. Within a decade de Broglie gave the electron a wave nature, and Heisenberg proved you cannot know its exact position and momentum at once.
And a strict limit to remember: Bohr's model works only for one-electron, hydrogen-like species $-$ hydrogen, helium plus, lithium two-plus, beryllium three-plus. A second electron breaks it.
For anything large, like a cricket ball, the wave nature is unimaginably tiny and unobservable $-$ which is exactly why the everyday world looks reassuringly classical.
Niels Bohr ने nineteen thirteen mein staircase picture ko kuch bold rules wale model mein badal diya.
Unhone declare kiya ki electron nucleus ke around sirf kuch stationary orbits mein ghoomta hai jahaan, saari classical expectation ke khilaaf, wo energy radiate karta hi नहीं.
Har aisi orbit ka fixed radius aur fixed energy hoti hai, aur electron sirf tab radiate karta hai jab wo orbits ke beech jump karta hai.

Kaunsi orbits allowed hain, ye tay karne ke liye Bohr ने ek quantisation rule joड़a: angular momentum sirf h over two pi ka whole-number multiple ho sakta hai, aur wahi integer n steps ko label karta hai.
Ye spectacularly kaam kiya. Isne hydrogen ki har spectral line ki exact wavelength predict kar di, jo ek model ke liye hairaan karne wali baat hai.

Par ye ek brilliant patch tha, final theory नहीं. Ek dashak ke andar de Broglie ने electron ko wave nature di, aur Heisenberg ने prove kiya ki aap uski exact position aur momentum ek saath नहीं jaan sakte.

Aur ek strict limit yaad rakho: Bohr ka model sirf one-electron, hydrogen-like species par kaam karta hai $-$ hydrogen, helium plus, lithium two-plus, beryllium three-plus. Doosra electron ise tod deta hai.
Kisi bhi bade cheez ke liye, jaise cricket ball, wave nature itni tiny hai ki dikhti hi नहीं $-$ isiliye rozmarra duniya reassuringly classical lagti hai.

sections.title: Deriving the Bohr radius

board_events.text: Radius: Coulomb pull $=$ centripetal need
The only inward force is electrostatic, so it must supply the centripetal force.
Now add Bohr's new rule: $m v r = \dfrac{n h}{2\pi} \Rightarrow v = \dfrac{n h}{2\pi m r}$.
$r \propto n^2$ and $r \propto 1/Z$; put $n=1, Z=1 \Rightarrow 0.529$ \AA $-$ real hydrogen.
Substitute the quantised $v$ into the force balance and solve for $r$ $-$ that is the whole derivation.

segments.text: This is the derivation hub of the chapter, and the radius comes first because everything else builds on it.
Start from the physical picture. The electron is held in its circular orbit because the Coulomb attraction from the nucleus supplies exactly the centripetal force it needs.
That is the key idea: the nucleus is a fixed positive charge, and the only inward force available is electrostatic, so it must do the job of keeping the electron curving.
Rearranging gives m-v-squared equal to the Coulomb term $-$ a clean expression for the kinetic part we will reuse in the energy derivation.
Now bring in Bohr's new rule that classical physics did not have: quantised angular momentum, which lets us write the speed in terms of n and r.
Substitute that speed back into the force balance, solve for r, and out drops the radius of the n-th orbit: about zero point five two nine times n-squared over Z ångström.
Read the result: radius grows as n-squared and shrinks as one over Z. Put n equals one and Z equals one and you get zero point five two nine ångström.
That is the size of a real hydrogen atom $-$ the model's very first triumph, and a strong sign Bohr was onto something real.
Ye chapter ka derivation hub hai, aur radius pehle aata hai kyunki baaki sab isi par bana hai.
Physical picture se shuru karo. Electron apni circular orbit mein isliye tika hai kyunki nucleus ka Coulomb attraction bilkul wahi centripetal force deta hai jiski use zaroorat hai.
Yahi key idea hai: nucleus ek fixed positive charge hai, aur ekmaatr inward force electrostatic hai, toh usi ko electron ko curve karate rehna hai.
Rearrange karo toh m-v-squared barabar Coulomb term $-$ kinetic hisse ki ek clean expression jise hum energy derivation mein dobara use karenge.
Ab Bohr ka wo naya rule laao jo classical physics ke paas नहीं tha: quantised angular momentum, jo humein speed ko n aur r ke terms mein likhne deta hai.
Us speed ko force balance mein wapas daalo, r ke liye solve karo, aur n-th orbit ka radius nikal aata hai: lagbhag zero point five two nine times n-squared over Z angstrom.
Result padho: radius n-squared ke saath badhta hai aur one over Z ke saath ghatta hai. n barabar one aur Z barabar one daalo toh zero point five two nine angstrom milta hai.
Ye ek asli hydrogen atom ka size hai $-$ model ki pehli hi jeet, aur ek strong ishaara ki Bohr kisi asli cheez par tha.

sections.title: Energy of the orbit: the KE and PE split

board_events.text: Energy: kinetic plus potential in the well
PE is negative: it takes work to pull the electron to infinity $-$ it sits in a well below zero.
Memorise: $\text{PE} = -2\,\text{KE}$ and $E = -\text{KE}$.
Negative, $1/n^2$-spaced levels are exactly the staircase from the intuition section.

segments.text: With the radius in hand, the energy follows by adding the electron's two energies: kinetic because it moves, and potential because it sits in the nucleus's attractive field.
The kinetic energy comes straight from the force balance we already found $-$ half m-v-squared equals that Coulomb term with an eight in the denominator.
The potential energy of the electron at distance r is the familiar Coulomb potential, and it carries a minus sign.
Why negative? Because it takes work to pull the electron away to infinity, so a bound electron sits in an energy well below zero.
Add the kinetic and potential energies and the total collapses neatly to a single negative term.
Substituting the radius gives the clean result: energy equals minus thirteen point six times Z-squared over n-squared electron-volts.
Two relations are worth memorising: the potential energy is minus twice the kinetic energy, and the total energy is just minus the kinetic energy.
These negative, one-over-n-squared-spaced levels are exactly the staircase we pictured at the start $-$ now with real numbers attached.
Radius haath mein aane ke baad, energy electron ki do energies jodkar nikalti hai: kinetic kyunki wo chalta hai, aur potential kyunki wo nucleus ke attractive field mein baitha hai.
Kinetic energy seedhe us force balance se aati hai jo hum pehle nikaal chuke $-$ half m-v-squared barabar wahi Coulomb term jismein denominator mein aath hai.
Distance r par electron ki potential energy wahi jaani-pehchaani Coulomb potential hai, aur ispe minus sign lagta hai.
Minus kyun? Kyunki electron ko infinity tak kheenchne mein work lagta hai, toh bound electron zero se neeche ek energy well mein baitha hai.
Kinetic aur potential energy jodo toh total saaf-suthre ek single negative term mein simat jaata hai.
Radius substitute karo toh clean result aata hai: energy barabar minus thirteen point six times Z-squared over n-squared electron-volts.
Do relations yaad rakhne layak hain: potential energy barabar minus two times kinetic energy, aur total energy bas minus kinetic energy.
Ye negative, one-over-n-squared-spaced levels bilkul wahi staircase hain jo humne shuru mein imagine ki thi $-$ ab asli numbers ke saath.

board_events.text: From energy gaps to the Rydberg equation
A drop from level $n_2$ to $n_1$ emits a photon carrying exactly the gap: $\Delta E = h\nu = hc/\lambda$.
$R_H = \dfrac{m e^4}{8\varepsilon_0^2 h^3 c}$ $-$ a fitted constant now emerges from fundamentals.

board_events.text: Fixed $n_1$ generates a named series: Lyman (1, UV), Balmer (2, visible), Paschen (3, IR), and so on.
This is Bohr's climax: predicting real spectral wavelengths from first principles.

segments.text: Now the payoff $-$ turning those energy levels into the spectral lines that started the whole story.
When an electron falls from a higher level to a lower one, energy conservation says the emitted photon carries exactly the gap between them.
Substituting the hydrogen energy expression, the photon energy equals two point one eight times ten to the minus eighteen joules, times the difference of the two inverse-square terms.
Divide through by h-c and you recover the experimentally known Rydberg form: the wavenumber equals the Rydberg constant times that same bracket.
Here is the climax. The Rydberg constant, originally just a number fitted to spectral data, now emerges from fundamental constants like the electron mass and charge.
Look at the level diagram: transitions ending on level one are the Lyman series, on level two the Balmer, on level three the Paschen.
So each fixed lower level generates a named series $-$ Lyman in the ultraviolet, Balmer in the visible, Paschen in the infrared, and onward.
<excited>This is Bohr's crowning achievement: he predicted the real, measured wavelengths of hydrogen's lines purely from first principles.</excited>
Ab payoff $-$ un energy levels ko un spectral lines mein badalna jinse poori kahani shuru hui thi.
Jab electron ऊpar wale level se neeche wale par girta hai, energy conservation kehta hai ki nikla photon un dono ke beech ka exact gap carry karta hai.
Hydrogen energy expression substitute karo toh photon energy barabar two point one eight times ten to the minus eighteen joules, times dono inverse-square terms ka difference.
H-c se divide karo toh aap experimentally known Rydberg form paate ho: wavenumber barabar Rydberg constant times wahi bracket.
Ye rahा climax. Rydberg constant, jo pehle sirf spectral data se fit kiya gaya ek number tha, ab electron mass aur charge jaise fundamental constants se nikal aata hai.
Level diagram dekho: level one par khatam hone wali transitions Lyman series hain, level two par Balmer, level three par Paschen.
Toh har fixed lower level ek named series banata hai $-$ Lyman ultraviolet mein, Balmer visible mein, Paschen infrared mein, aur aage.
<excited>Ye Bohr ki taaj wali uplabdhi hai: usne hydrogen ki lines ki asli, measured wavelengths sirf first principles se predict kar di.</excited>

sections.title: de Broglie derives Bohr's quantisation

board_events.text: Why the quantisation rule is not magic
Treat the orbiting electron as a standing wave wrapped around the orbit $-$ like a guitar string bent into a loop.
For the wave to survive, the circumference must hold a WHOLE number of wavelengths.

board_events.text: Exactly Bohr's angular-momentum rule $-$ Bohr assumed it, de Broglie DERIVED it.
The integer $n$ is simply the count of whole electron-waves fitting around the orbit.

segments.text: Here is why de Broglie's idea is far more than a curiosity $-$ it explains where Bohr's mysterious rule actually comes from.
Treat the orbiting electron not as a tiny ball but as a standing wave wrapped around the circular orbit, like a guitar string bent into a closed loop.
For that wave to survive rather than cancel itself by interference, the circumference must hold a whole number of wavelengths.
Write that condition directly: two pi r equals n times the wavelength.
Now substitute the de Broglie wavelength, h over m-v, and rearrange $-$ and out comes m-v-r equals n times h over two pi.
Look at the picture: the wave closes on itself smoothly only when a whole number of humps fit around the loop.
That result is exactly Bohr's angular-momentum rule. Bohr had simply assumed it as a postulate; de Broglie derived it from the electron's wave nature.
So the integer n is no longer a magic number $-$ it is just the count of whole electron-waves that fit around the orbit.
Ye rahी wajah ki de Broglie ka idea sirf ek curiosity se kahin zyaada hai $-$ ye batata hai ki Bohr ka mysterious rule asal mein aata kahaan se hai.
Orbiting electron ko ek tiny ball ki tarah नहीं balki circular orbit ke around lipti ek standing wave ki tarah maano, jaise guitar string ek closed loop mein muड़ी ho.
Us wave ke survive karne ke liye, interference se khud ko cancel karne ke bajaye, circumference mein poora number wavelengths hone chahiye.
Wo condition seedhe likho: two pi r barabar n times wavelength.
Ab de Broglie wavelength, h over m-v, substitute karo aur rearrange karo $-$ aur nikal aata hai m-v-r barabar n times h over two pi.
Picture dekho: wave khud par tabhi smoothly band hoti hai jab poora number humps loop ke around fit ho jaayein.
Wo result bilkul Bohr ka angular-momentum rule hai. Bohr ne ise bas ek postulate maan liya tha; de Broglie ne ise electron ki wave nature se derive kar diya.
Toh integer n ab koi magic number नहीं $-$ ye bas poore electron-waves ki ginti hai jo orbit ke around fit hote hain.

sections.title: Why Bohr's model still fails

board_events.text: The four cracks in Bohr's model
It works only for one-electron species; a second electron brings repulsion Bohr never accounted for.
It cannot predict helium or any multi-electron spectrum.
It cannot explain line splitting in magnetic (Zeeman) or electric (Stark) fields.
It cannot explain chemical bonding.
Most deeply: a definite orbit means a definite position AND velocity $-$ violating Heisenberg.
By assigning a sharp path, Bohr ignores the electron's wave nature.
These failures are the doorway to the quantum-mechanical model of the next subtopic.

segments.text: For all its brilliance, Bohr's picture breaks down, and knowing exactly how is a favourite exam theme.
The first crack: it works only for one-electron species. The moment a second electron appears, electron-electron repulsion, which Bohr never accounted for, wrecks the model.
So it cannot predict the spectrum of neutral helium or any multi-electron atom $-$ a serious limitation.
The second: it cannot explain why spectral lines split in a magnetic field, the Zeeman effect, or in an electric field, the Stark effect.
The third: it says nothing about chemical bonding, which is central to all of chemistry.

The deepest failure is conceptual. By assigning the electron a definite orbit, Bohr gives it a definite position and a definite velocity at once $-$ which directly violates Heisenberg's uncertainty principle.
In doing so, the model ignores the electron's wave nature that de Broglie had just revealed.
These four failures are not an ending $-$ they are the doorway to the full quantum-mechanical model of the next subtopic.
Apni saari brilliance ke bawajood, Bohr ka picture toot jaata hai, aur exactly kaise, ye ek pasandeeda exam theme hai.
Pehli crack: ye sirf one-electron species par kaam karta hai. Jaise hi doosra electron aata hai, electron-electron repulsion, jo Bohr ne kabhi account नहीं kiya, model ko bigaad deta hai.
Toh ye neutral helium ya kisi bhi multi-electron atom ka spectrum predict नहीं kar sakta $-$ ek serious limitation.
Doosri: ye नहीं bata sakta ki spectral lines magnetic field mein kyun split hoti hain, Zeeman effect, ya electric field mein, Stark effect.
Teesri: ye chemical bonding ke baare mein kuch नहीं kehta, jo poori chemistry ka central hissa hai.

Sabse gehri failure conceptual hai. Electron ko ek definite orbit dekar, Bohr use ek saath definite position aur definite velocity de deta hai $-$ jo seedhe Heisenberg ke uncertainty principle ka violation hai.
Aisa karke, model electron ki us wave nature ko ignore karta hai jise de Broglie ne abhi reveal kiya tha.
Ye chaar failures ek ant नहीं $-$ ye agle subtopic ke poore quantum-mechanical model ka darwaaza hain.

sections.title: The four scaling laws

board_events.text: The four scaling laws (hydrogen-like)
$r \propto n^2/Z$, $E \propto Z^2/n^2$, $v \propto Z/n$, $\bar{\nu} \propto Z^2$.
Most $Z$-comparison questions are solved by these ratios alone $-$ no full calculation.
The Bohr radius $a_0 = 0.529$ \AA\ is the hydrogen ground state ($n=1, Z=1$).

segments.text: Here is the reference toolkit for Bohr numericals $-$ four scaling relations that, once memorised, solve most questions in seconds.
First, the quantisation rule itself: angular momentum is a whole-number multiple of h over two pi.
The radius of the n-th orbit is zero point five two nine times n-squared over Z ångström, which is fifty-two point nine times the same in picometres.
The energy is minus thirteen point six times Z-squared over n-squared electron-volts, or equivalently minus two point one eight times ten to the minus eighteen joules with the same ratio.
The orbital speed is two point one eight times ten to the six times Z over n metres per second.
Strip these to their proportionalities: radius as n-squared over Z, energy as Z-squared over n-squared, speed as Z over n, and wavenumber as Z-squared.
That is the real time-saver: most Z-comparison questions fall to these ratios alone, with no full calculation needed.
And keep one landmark fixed: the Bohr radius, zero point five two nine ångström, is the hydrogen ground state with n and Z both equal to one.
Ye rahा Bohr numericals ka reference toolkit $-$ chaar scaling relations jo, ek baar yaad ho jaayein, zyaadatar sawaal seconds mein solve karte hain.
Pehle quantisation rule khud: angular momentum h over two pi ka whole-number multiple hai.
N-th orbit ka radius zero point five two nine times n-squared over Z angstrom hai, jo picometres mein fifty-two point nine times wahi hai.
Energy minus thirteen point six times Z-squared over n-squared electron-volts hai, ya equivalently minus two point one eight times ten to the minus eighteen joules ussi ratio ke saath.
Orbital speed two point one eight times ten to the six times Z over n metres per second hai.
Inhe unki proportionalities tak simplify karo: radius as n-squared over Z, energy as Z-squared over n-squared, speed as Z over n, aur wavenumber as Z-squared.
Yahi asli time-saver hai: zyaadatar Z-comparison sawaal sirf in ratios se nikal jaate hain, bina poore calculation ke.
Aur ek landmark fix rakho: Bohr radius, zero point five two nine angstrom, hydrogen ground state hai jismein n aur Z dono barabar one.

sections.title: Rydberg, series, de Broglie, and Heisenberg

board_events.text: Spectra, matter waves, and uncertainty
$R_H = 1.097\times10^{7}$ m$^{-1}$. Series: Lyman(1), Balmer(2), Paschen(3), Brackett(4), Pfund(5).
de Broglie waves matter only for light, fast particles; for a cricket ball $\lambda$ is unobservably tiny.
Uncertainty forbids a definite orbit $-$ the death blow to Bohr's sharp path.

segments.text: The second half of the toolkit covers spectra, matter waves, and uncertainty $-$ the trio that both crowns and buries Bohr.
The Rydberg equation gives the wavenumber of any hydrogen-like line: the Rydberg constant times Z-squared, times the difference of the two inverse-square terms, with the upper level larger.
The Rydberg constant is about one point zero nine seven times ten to the seven per metre, and the named series run Lyman, Balmer, Paschen, Brackett, Pfund for lower levels one through five.
A handy counting formula: an electron cascading from level n down to the ground state produces n times n minus one, all over two, distinct lines.
The de Broglie wavelength is h over the momentum, which you can also write using kinetic energy, or the accelerating voltage for a charged particle.
But matter waves only matter for light, fast particles like electrons. For a cricket ball the wavelength is unimaginably tiny and never observed.
Finally, Heisenberg's uncertainty principle: the product of the uncertainties in position and momentum cannot fall below h over four pi.
That single inequality forbids a definite orbit with a fixed radius $-$ it is the quiet death blow to Bohr's sharp planetary path.
Toolkit ka doosra hissa spectra, matter waves aur uncertainty cover karta hai $-$ wo teen jo Bohr ko taaj bhi pehnaate hain aur dafn bhi karte hain.
Rydberg equation kisi bhi hydrogen-like line ka wavenumber deta hai: Rydberg constant times Z-squared, times dono inverse-square terms ka difference, upper level bada hone ke saath.
Rydberg constant lagbhag one point zero nine seven times ten to the seven per metre hai, aur named series Lyman, Balmer, Paschen, Brackett, Pfund chalti hain lower levels one se five ke liye.
Ek handy counting formula: level n se ground state tak cascade karta electron n times n minus one, poora over two, distinct lines banata hai.
De Broglie wavelength h over momentum hai, jise aap kinetic energy se, ya charged particle ke liye accelerating voltage se bhi likh sakte ho.
Par matter waves sirf light, fast particles jaise electrons ke liye matter karte hain. Cricket ball ke liye wavelength itni tiny hai ki kabhi observe नहीं hoti.
Aakhir mein Heisenberg ka uncertainty principle: position aur momentum ki uncertainties ka product h over four pi se neeche नहीं gir sakta.
Wo ek inequality fixed radius wale definite orbit ko forbid karti hai $-$ ye Bohr ke sharp planetary path ka chupka death blow hai.

sections.title: Worked example (CBSE): radius and energy of He+ (n=3)

board_events.text: [CBSE] Radius and energy, He$^+$, $n=3$
He$^+$ so $Z = 2$; the third orbit $n = 3$. Take $a_0 = 0.529$ \AA.
Use the scaling forms directly $-$ no need to rebuild from constants.
The negative energy confirms the electron is bound.
Answer: radius $2.38$ \AA, energy $-6.04$ eV.
Plug $n$ and $Z$ into $n^2/Z$ and $Z^2/n^2$ $-$ that is the entire method.

segments.text: Let us start Bohr's worked examples with a clean board-level plug-in that just exercises the scaling laws.
We want the radius and energy of the third orbit of the helium-plus ion, so the atomic number is two and n is three.
For the radius, use zero point five two nine times n-squared over Z. That is zero point five two nine times nine over two, which gives two point three eight ångström.
For the energy, use minus thirteen point six times Z-squared over n-squared. That is minus thirteen point six times four over nine, which is minus six point zero four electron-volts.
Notice we never rebuilt anything from fundamental constants $-$ the scaling forms do all the work directly.
The energy comes out negative, which is the reassuring sign that the electron is bound to the nucleus.
So the answers are a radius of two point three eight ångström and an energy of minus six point zero four electron-volts.
The whole method is just plugging n and Z into n-squared over Z and Z-squared over n-squared. Memorise the two ratios and this becomes automatic.
Bohr ke worked examples ek clean board-level plug-in se shuru karein jo bas scaling laws ka abhyaas karaata hai.
Humein helium-plus ion ki teesri orbit ka radius aur energy chahiye, toh atomic number two hai aur n three.
Radius ke liye zero point five two nine times n-squared over Z use karo. Wo zero point five two nine times nine over two, jo two point three eight angstrom deta hai.
Energy ke liye minus thirteen point six times Z-squared over n-squared use karo. Wo minus thirteen point six times four over nine, jo minus six point zero four electron-volts hai.
Dhyaan do ki humne kuch bhi fundamental constants se dobara नहीं banaya $-$ scaling forms saara kaam seedhe kar dete hain.
Energy negative aati hai, jo reassuring sign hai ki electron nucleus se bound hai.
Toh jawaab hain two point three eight angstrom radius aur minus six point zero four electron-volts energy.
Poora method bas n aur Z ko n-squared over Z aur Z-squared over n-squared mein daalna hai. Do ratios yaad karo aur ye automatic ho jaata hai.

sections.title: Worked example (NEET): same transition, different ion

board_events.text: [NEET] Lyman line for He$^+$ by scaling
The first Lyman line of hydrogen is at 1216 \AA. Find it for He$^+$.
The trap: relaunching the full Rydberg calculation for He$^+$.
For the same transition, $\bar{\nu} \propto Z^2$, so $\lambda \propto 1/Z^2$.
Answer: 304 \AA $-$ in about ten seconds.
The whole game is the $Z^2$ scaling; never recompute from scratch.

segments.text: This is a pure speed question, and the trick is to lean entirely on the Z-squared scaling.
We are told the first Lyman line of hydrogen sits at one thousand two hundred sixteen ångström, and we want the same line for the helium-plus ion.
The trap is to relaunch the full Rydberg calculation for helium-plus, which burns two minutes for no reason.
Instead, recall that for the same transition the wavenumber scales as Z-squared, so the wavelength scales as one over Z-squared.
The ratio of helium-plus wavelength to hydrogen wavelength is the hydrogen Z-squared over the helium Z-squared, which is one over four.
So just divide the hydrogen wavelength by four: one thousand two hundred sixteen over four gives three hundred four ångström.
That is the answer, three hundred four ångström, reached in about ten seconds.
The whole game is the Z-squared scaling. Whenever you see the same transition in a different ion, scale $-$ never recompute from scratch.
Ye ek pure speed sawaal hai, aur trick ye hai ki poori tarah Z-squared scaling par tik jao.
Humein bataya gaya ki hydrogen ki pehli Lyman line one thousand two hundred sixteen angstrom par hai, aur humein helium-plus ion ke liye wahi line chahiye.
Trap ye hai ki helium-plus ke liye poora Rydberg calculation dobara chalao, jo bina wajah do minute barbaad karta hai.
Iske bajaye yaad karo ki same transition ke liye wavenumber Z-squared ke saath scale hota hai, toh wavelength one over Z-squared ke saath.
Helium-plus wavelength ka hydrogen wavelength se ratio barabar hydrogen Z-squared over helium Z-squared, jo one over four hai.
Toh bas hydrogen wavelength ko four se divide karo: one thousand two hundred sixteen over four, jo three hundred four angstrom deta hai.
Yahi jawaab hai, three hundred four angstrom, lagbhag das second mein.
Poora khel Z-squared scaling hai. Jab bhi alag ion mein same transition dikhe, scale karo $-$ scratch se dobara kabhi mat karo.

sections.title: Worked example (JEE Main): standing wave in the n=2 orbit

board_events.text: [JEE Main] de Broglie wave in the $n=2$ orbit
For $n=2$ in hydrogen, find $\lambda$ and show the circumference is an integer number of them. Take $v_1 = 2.18\times10^6$ m s$^{-1}$.
Exactly two de Broglie wavelengths fit the $n=2$ orbit.
A direct confirmation of the standing-wave derivation.

segments.text: This example turns the standing-wave idea into an actual numerical check, which is exactly what J E E Main likes.
For the second orbit of hydrogen we must find the de Broglie wavelength and then show the orbit circumference holds a whole number of them.
First the speed. Bohr's velocity scales as one over n, so the second-orbit speed is the ground-state speed divided by two, about one point zero nine times ten to the six metres per second.
Now the de Broglie wavelength is h over m-v-two. Plugging in gives about six point six eight times ten to the minus ten metres.

Next the circumference. The second-orbit radius is zero point five two nine times four, about two point one two ångström, so two pi r is about one point three three times ten to the minus nine metres.
Divide the circumference by the wavelength and you get almost exactly two, which is the value of n.
So precisely two de Broglie wavelengths fit around the second orbit $-$ no more, no less.
This is a direct, hands-on confirmation of the standing-wave derivation we did earlier: the integer n really is the number of waves that fit.
Ye example standing-wave idea ko ek asli numerical check mein badal deta hai, jo bilkul wahi hai jo J E E Main ko pasand hai.
Hydrogen ki doosri orbit ke liye humein de Broglie wavelength nikalni hai aur phir dikhana hai ki orbit circumference mein poora number wavelengths samaate hain.
Pehle speed. Bohr ki velocity one over n ke saath scale hoti hai, toh doosri-orbit speed ground-state speed divided by two hai, lagbhag one point zero nine times ten to the six metres per second.
Ab de Broglie wavelength h over m-v-two hai. Daalne par lagbhag six point six eight times ten to the minus ten metres aata hai.
Aage circumference. Doosri-orbit radius zero point five two nine times four, lagbhag two point one two angstrom, toh two pi r lagbhag one point three three times ten to the minus nine metres.
Circumference ko wavelength se divide karo toh lagbhag exactly two milta hai, jo n ka value hai.
Toh theek two de Broglie wavelengths doosri orbit ke around fit hote hain $-$ na zyaada, na kam.
Ye pehle ki gayi standing-wave derivation ka ek direct, hands-on confirmation hai: integer n sach mein un waves ki sankhya hai jo fit hote hain.

sections.title: Worked example (JEE Advanced): line count to shortest wavelength

board_events.text: [JEE Advanced] Line count $\to$ $n$ $\to$ shortest wavelength
A hydrogen-like ion, excited from the ground state, emits 6 distinct lines. Find $n$; then for He$^+$ the absorbed-photon energy and the shortest emitted wavelength.
The shortest wavelength is the largest emission gap $-$ the direct $n=4 \to n=1$ drop, again $51.0$ eV.
Chain: line count $\to n \to$ energy levels $\to$ photon wavelength.

segments.text: This is the signature J E E Advanced structure, chaining three ideas into one clean cascade.

A hydrogen-like ion is excited from its ground state and, on de-exciting, emits six distinct spectral lines. We must find the excited level, then for helium-plus the absorbed-photon energy and the shortest emitted wavelength.
Step one uses the line-count formula. Setting n times n minus one over two equal to six gives n times n minus one equal to twelve, so n is four.
Step two finds the energies for helium-plus, with Z equal to two. The ground level is minus fifty-four point four electron-volts and the fourth level is minus three point four.
The absorbed photon drove the one-to-four jump, so its energy is the difference, fifty-one point zero electron-volts.
For the shortest emitted wavelength, we need the largest energy gap in emission, which is the direct four-to-one drop $-$ releasing that same fifty-one electron-volts.
Convert with the shortcut: twelve hundred forty over fifty-one gives about twenty-four point three nanometres, deep in the far ultraviolet.
So the chain is the whole lesson: line count gives n, n gives the energy levels, and the energy gap gives the photon wavelength.
Ye signature J E E Advanced structure hai, teen ideas ko ek clean cascade mein chain karta hua.

Ek hydrogen-like ion apne ground state se excite hota hai aur, de-excite karte hue, chhe distinct spectral lines emit karta hai. Humein excited level nikalna hai, phir helium-plus ke liye absorbed-photon energy aur sabse chhoti emitted wavelength.
Step one line-count formula use karta hai. n times n minus one over two barabar six rakho toh n times n minus one barabar twelve, toh n four hai.
Step two helium-plus ke liye energies nikalta hai, Z barabar two ke saath. Ground level minus fifty-four point four electron-volts hai aur chautha level minus three point four.
Absorbed photon ne one-to-four jump karaya, toh uski energy difference hai, fifty-one point zero electron-volts.
Sabse chhoti emitted wavelength ke liye humein emission ka sabse bada energy gap chahiye, jo direct four-to-one drop hai $-$ wahi fifty-one electron-volts release karta.
Shortcut se convert karo: twelve hundred forty over fifty-one lagbhag twenty-four point three nanometres deta hai, gehre far ultraviolet mein.
Toh chain hi poora sabak hai: line count se n, n se energy levels, aur energy gap se photon wavelength.

sections.title: Pitfalls and pro-tips: Bohr and duality

board_events.text: Bohr traps to dodge
Pitfall 1: wrong power in scaling $-$ $r \propto n^2/Z$, $E \propto Z^2/n^2$, $v \propto Z/n$, $\bar{\nu} \propto Z^2$.
Pitfall 2: miscounting lines $-$ from level $n$ to ground it is $\dfrac{n(n-1)}{2}$, not $n-1$.
Pitfall 3: applying Bohr to multi-electron atoms $-$ valid only for H, He$^+$, Li$^{2+}$, Be$^{3+}$.
Pitfall 4: dropping the negative sign $-$ orbit energies are ALWAYS negative.
Energy absorbed going up is positive; energy released coming down is positive; but $E_n$ itself stays negative.
Pro-tip: same transition, different ion $-$ $\lambda \propto 1/Z^2$, $E \propto Z^2$; never recompute.
Series order: Lyman UV, Balmer visible, the rest IR; lower $n_1$ means higher energy.

segments.text: Let us close this heavyweight subtopic with the four traps that repeatedly cost marks, and the pro-tip that turns hard problems into ratios.
The first trap is the wrong power in the scaling laws. Lock them in: radius as n-squared over Z, energy as Z-squared over n-squared, speed as Z over n, and wavenumber as Z-squared.
The second is miscounting spectral lines. From an excited level n down to the ground state, the count is n times n minus one over two, not simply n minus one.

The third is applying Bohr where it does not belong. Its equations are valid only for one-electron species $-$ hydrogen, helium plus, lithium two-plus, beryllium three-plus. Check the electron count, not just a simple-looking symbol.
The fourth is dropping the negative sign on energy. Orbit energies are always negative because the electron is bound.
Be precise about signs: energy absorbed on an upward jump is positive, energy released on a downward jump is positive, but the level energy itself always stays negative.
<whisper>Here is the pro-tip: for any same-transition, different-ion problem, wavelength scales as one over Z-squared and energy as Z-squared. Never recompute from scratch.</whisper>
And keep the series map ready: Lyman is ultraviolet, Balmer visible, the rest infrared, and a lower final level always means higher energy.
Chalo is heavyweight subtopic ko un chaar traps ke saath band karein jo baar-baar marks le lete hain, aur wo pro-tip jo mushkil problems ko ratios mein badal deta hai.
Pehla trap scaling laws mein galat power hai. Inhe lock karo: radius as n-squared over Z, energy as Z-squared over n-squared, speed as Z over n, aur wavenumber as Z-squared.
Doosra spectral lines miscount karna hai. Excited level n se ground state tak, count n times n minus one over two hai, sirf n minus one नहीं.

Teesra Bohr ko wahaan apply karna hai jahaan wo belong नहीं karta. Iske equations sirf one-electron species ke liye valid hain $-$ hydrogen, helium plus, lithium two-plus, beryllium three-plus. Electron count check karo, sirf simple dikhne wala symbol नहीं.
Chautha energy par negative sign gira dena hai. Orbit energies hamesha negative hoti hain kyunki electron bound hai.
Signs ke baare mein precise raho: upward jump par absorbed energy positive, downward jump par released energy positive, par level energy khud hamesha negative rehti hai.

<whisper>Ye rahा pro-tip: kisi bhi same-transition, different-ion problem ke liye, wavelength one over Z-squared ke saath scale hoti hai aur energy Z-squared ke saath. Scratch se dobara kabhi mat karo.</whisper>
Aur series map ready rakho: Lyman ultraviolet, Balmer visible, baaki infrared, aur lower final level hamesha higher energy ka matlab hai.

sections.title: From orbit to orbital: Schrodinger's probability cloud

board_events.text: From orbit to orbital
Heisenberg killed the definite path, so the sharp orbit had to go.
Schr\"odinger (1926) wrote a wave equation for the electron; solving it gives a wave function $\psi$.
$\psi^2$ = the probability of finding the electron at each point $-$ certainty traded for probability.
Instead of a thin wire-like orbit, we get a fuzzy 3-D cloud of probability: an orbital.

board_events.text: Like a spinning fan blade, you cannot point to the electron $-$ only to the region it likely occupies.
An orbital is a region of likely presence, NEVER a path the electron travels.

segments.text: We ended the last subtopic with Bohr in ruins: de Broglie gave the electron a wave nature, and Heisenberg forbade knowing its exact position and momentum at once.
Bohr's whole picture rested on a sharp circular orbit, a definite path. If you cannot know where the electron is and how fast it moves, a definite path is a fiction, so the orbit had to go.
Erwin Schrödinger, in nineteen twenty-six, wrote down a wave equation for the electron. We will not solve it, but its meaning is everything: solving it gives a wave function, written psi.
The square of that function tells you the probability of finding the electron at each point in space. We trade certainty for probability.
So instead of a thin, wire-like orbit, we get a fuzzy three-dimensional cloud of probability around the nucleus $-$ and that cloud is what we call an orbital.
Picture the cloud: densest near the nucleus and fading outward, where the electron is most likely to be found.
Think of a ceiling fan at full speed. You cannot point to where a single blade is at any instant, but you can describe the disc it sweeps out $-$ the region it is likely to occupy.
That is exactly an orbital: not a path the electron follows, but a region of space where the electron is likely to be found.
Pichhle subtopic ko humne Bohr ke khandahar ke saath chhoda: de Broglie ने electron ko wave nature di, aur Heisenberg ने ek saath uski exact position aur momentum jaanna forbid kar diya.

Bohr ka poora picture ek sharp circular orbit, ek definite path par tika tha. Agar aap जान hi नहीं sakte ki electron kahaan hai aur kitni tezी se chal raha hai, toh definite path ek fiction hai, toh orbit ko jaana hi tha.

Erwin Schrodinger ने, nineteen twenty-six mein, electron ke liye ek wave equation likhi. Hum ise solve नहीं karenge, par iska matlab sab kuch hai: ise solve karne par ek wave function milta hai, jise psi likhte hain.
Us function ka square aapko har point par electron milne ki probability batata hai. Hum certainty ko probability se badal dete hain.
Toh ek patli, wire-jaisi orbit ke bajaye, humein nucleus ke around ek fuzzy three-dimensional probability ka cloud milta hai $-$ aur usi cloud ko hum orbital kehte hain.
Cloud ko imagine karo: nucleus ke paas sabse dense aur bahar ki taraf fade hota, jahaan electron milne ki sabse zyaada sambhavna hai.

Ek ceiling fan ko full speed par socho. Aap kisi ek instant par ek single blade kahaan hai ye point नहीं kar sakte, par aap us disc ko describe kar sakte ho jise wo sweep karta hai $-$ wo region jise wo likely occupy karta hai.
Orbital bilkul yahi hai: koi path jise electron follow karta ho aisa नहीं, balki space ka wo region jahaan electron milne ki sambhavna ho.

sections.title: The electron's postal address: four quantum numbers and orbital shapes

board_events.text: The electron's postal address
Every orbital is labelled by quantum numbers that fall out of Schr\"odinger's equation.
$n$ = the city (shell); $l$ = the street (subshell / shape); $m_l$ = the house; $m_s$ = the seat.
No two electrons share the same full address $-$ Pauli's rule, the root of atomic structure.
Shape is fixed by $l$: an $s$ orbital ($l=0$) is a sphere; a $p$ orbital ($l=1$) is a dumbbell.

segments.text: A fan disc is fully described by a few numbers $-$ its radius, its tilt, its height. In the same way, every orbital is completely labelled by a set of quantum numbers.
These numbers are not arbitrary; they fall out naturally when you solve Schrödinger's equation. Three describe the orbital and a fourth describes the electron's spin inside it.

Think of them as a postal address. The principal number is the city, that is the shell; the azimuthal number is the street, the subshell and its shape; the magnetic number is the house; and the spin number is which seat in that house.
One rule governs the whole address: no two electrons in an atom can share the same full set. That is Pauli's exclusion principle, and it is the root of all atomic structure.
What do the clouds look like? Their shape is set entirely by the azimuthal number. An s orbital, with l zero, is a simple sphere; a p orbital, with l one, is a dumbbell with two lobes.
Look at the three shapes: the round s, the two-lobed p dumbbell, and the four-lobed d cloverleaf.
A d orbital, with l two, has five members; an f orbital, with l three, has seven. The pattern is always two-l-plus-one orientations for each value of l.
Those orientations are simply the house numbers that the magnetic quantum number is allowed to take.
Ek fan disc kuch numbers se poori tarah describe ho jaati hai $-$ uska radius, tilt, height. Ussi tarah, har orbital quantum numbers ke ek set se poori tarah label hota hai.
Ye numbers arbitrary नहीं hain; ye Schrodinger ka equation solve karne par naturally nikalte hain. Teen orbital ko describe karte hain aur chautha uske andar electron ke spin ko.
Inhe ek postal address socho. Principal number city hai, yaani shell; azimuthal number street hai, subshell aur uski shape; magnetic number house hai; aur spin number us house mein kaunsi seat.
Ek rule poore address ko govern karta hai: atom mein koi do electrons same poora set share नहीं kar sakte. Ye Pauli ka exclusion principle hai, aur ye saari atomic structure ki jaड़ hai.
Clouds dikhte kaise hain? Unki shape poori tarah azimuthal number se tay hoti hai. Ek s orbital, l zero ke saath, ek simple sphere hai; ek p orbital, l one ke saath, do lobes wala dumbbell.
Teen shapes dekho: gol s, do-lobe wala p dumbbell, aur chaar-lobe wala d cloverleaf.
Ek d orbital, l two ke saath, paanch members rakhta hai; ek f orbital, l three ke saath, saat. Pattern hamesha two-l-plus-one orientations hai har l ke value ke liye.
Wo orientations bas wo house numbers hain jo magnetic quantum number le sakta hai.

sections.title: Seating the electrons: Aufbau, Pauli, Hund

board_events.text: Seating the electrons
Filling a multi-electron atom is like seating wedding guests.
Aufbau: fill the cheapest (lowest-energy) seats first.
Pauli: never seat two guests with an identical full address.
Hund: when several equal seats are open, everyone gets their own before doubling up.
Applied in order, these three rules generate every element's electronic configuration.
And through configuration, the entire structure of the periodic table.
The order of the seats comes from the $(n+l)$ rule, coming up next.

segments.text: Once we know the addresses available, filling a multi-electron atom is a lot like seating guests at a wedding.
There are three rules, and you apply them strictly in order.
The first is Aufbau: always fill the cheapest, lowest-energy seats first, before touching any higher one.
The second is Pauli: never seat two guests with an identical full address $-$ no two electrons may share all four quantum numbers.
The third is Hund: when several equal seats are open at one table, give everyone their own seat before anyone doubles up.
Applied in that order, these three rules generate the electronic configuration of every element in the table.
And through those configurations, the entire structure of the periodic table emerges $-$ periods, groups, and blocks all follow.
There is one thing still to pin down: exactly what order the seats fill in. That comes from the n-plus-l rule, which we take up next.
Jab hum jaan lete hain ki kaunse addresses available hain, toh ek multi-electron atom ko bharna kaafi kuch shaadi mein guests ko bithaane jaisa hai.
Teen rules hain, aur aap unhe sakhti se order mein apply karte ho.
Pehla Aufbau hai: hamesha sabse sasti, lowest-energy seats pehle bharo, kisi upar wali ko chhoone se pehle.
Doosra Pauli hai: kabhi do guests ko same poore address ke saath mat bithao $-$ koi do electrons saare chaar quantum numbers share नहीं kar sakte.
Teesra Hund hai: jab ek table par kai barabar seats khaali hon, toh koi double up kare usse pehle har kisi ko apni seat do.
Us order mein apply karo toh ye teen rules table ke har element ki electronic configuration bana dete hain.
Aur un configurations ke zariye, poore periodic table ki structure ubharti hai $-$ periods, groups aur blocks sab follow karte hain.
Ek cheez abhi tay karni baaki hai: seats exactly kis order mein bharti hain. Wo n-plus-l rule se aata hai, jise hum aage lenge.

sections.title: Assigning quantum numbers and counting nodes

board_events.text: Assigning $n, l, m_l, m_s$ and counting nodes
Work outward from $n$: allowed $l$ runs $0$ to $(n-1)$; allowed $m_l$ runs $-l$ to $+l$; then assign spin.
Each number's range is set by the one above $-$ fixing $m_l$ before $l$ is writing a house number before the street.
The total wiggle room is set by $n$; the angular part claims $l$ (the shape), the rest become spherical shells of zero probability.
Always check: radial $+$ angular $= n-1$. If they don't sum, you slipped.
A node is a surface where $\psi^2 = 0$ $-$ the electron is never found there.

segments.text: Now the procedural core of this subtopic: assigning the four quantum numbers cleanly, and counting nodes without slipping.
Work outward from the principal number. The allowed azimuthal values run from zero up to n minus one; the allowed magnetic values run from minus l to plus l; then you assign the spin.
The order matters because each number's range is set by the one above it. Trying to fix the magnetic number before the azimuthal is like writing a house number before you know the street.
For nodes, memorise three counts: radial nodes are n minus l minus one, angular nodes equal l, and the total is always n minus one.
The reasoning: the total wiggle room of the wave function is set by n. The angular part claims l of it, giving the shape, and whatever is left becomes spherical shells of zero probability.
Check it on a three-p orbital: l is one, so there is one angular node, and n minus l minus one gives one radial node, totalling two, which is n minus one.
That is your self-check every time: radial plus angular must equal n minus one. If they do not sum, you have slipped somewhere.
And keep the meaning in view: a node is a surface where psi-squared is zero, so the electron is simply never found there.
Ab is subtopic ka procedural core: chaaron quantum numbers ko saaf-suthre assign karna, aur nodes ko bina phisle count karna.
Principal number se bahar ki taraf kaam karo. Allowed azimuthal values zero se n minus one tak chalti hain; allowed magnetic values minus l se plus l tak; phir aap spin assign karte ho.
Order maayne rakhta hai kyunki har number ki range uske ऊpar wale se tay hoti hai. Azimuthal se pehle magnetic number fix karna aise hai jaise street jaane bina house number likhna.
Nodes ke liye teen counts yaad karo: radial nodes n minus l minus one, angular nodes barabar l, aur total hamesha n minus one.
Reasoning: wave function ka total wiggle room n se tay hota hai. Angular part usmein se l claim karta hai, shape deta hai, aur jo bache wo zero probability ke spherical shells ban jaate hain.
Ise ek three-p orbital par check karo: l one hai, toh ek angular node hai, aur n minus l minus one ek radial node deta hai, total two, jo n minus one hai.
Yahi har baar aapka self-check hai: radial plus angular barabar n minus one hona chahiye. Agar sum नहीं hote, toh aap kahin phisle ho.
Aur matlab nazar mein rakho: node ek surface hai jahaan psi-squared zero hai, toh electron wahaan kabhi milta hi नहीं.

sections.title: Ordering energies: the (n+l) rule and shielding

board_events.text: The $(n+l)$ rule and why it works
Compute $(n+l)$ for each subshell; the lower value fills first. Ties break by the lower $n$.
This is why 4s fills BEFORE 3d $-$ the famous ordering.
Physically: a higher $l$ is a more spread-out shape, poorly shielded, feeling less nuclear pull $-$ so its energy rises.
Within a shell an $s$ electron penetrates closest and is held tightest, then $p$, then $d$, then $f$.
So the effective nuclear charge felt DECREASES as $l$ increases $-$ that splits a shell's levels.
For a one-electron species, energy depends on $n$ alone $-$ know which regime you are in.

segments.text: Here is the rule that decides the filling order, and, just as important, the physical reason behind it.
For each subshell, compute n plus l. The subshell with the lower value fills first, and if two are tied, the one with the lower n wins.
Take the classic case. Four-s has n plus l equal to four, while three-d has n plus l equal to five.
Since four is less than five, four-s sinks below three-d and fills first. That is the famous four-s-before-three-d ordering that surprises so many students.
Why does it happen physically? A higher azimuthal number means a more spread-out shape that is poorly shielded and feels less of the nucleus, so its energy is pushed up.
Within a single shell, an s electron penetrates closest to the nucleus and is held most tightly, then p, then d, then f.
So the effective nuclear charge an electron feels decreases as the azimuthal number increases, and that is exactly what splits a shell into separate energy levels.
One caution: for a one-electron species there is no such splitting $-$ energy depends on n alone. Always know which regime you are in before applying the rule.
Ye rahा wo rule jo filling order tay karta hai, aur utni hi ahम, uske peeche ki physical wajah.
Har subshell ke liye n plus l compute karo. Jiska value kam ho wo subshell pehle bharti hai, aur agar do tie hon, toh kam n wala jeetta hai.
Classic case lo. Four-s ka n plus l barabar four hai, jabki three-d ka n plus l barabar five.
Kyunki four, five se kam hai, four-s three-d ke neeche dhas jaata hai aur pehle bharta hai. Yahi wo famous four-s-before-three-d ordering hai jo itne students ko chaunka deti hai.
Ye physically hota kyun hai? Zyaada azimuthal number matlab ek zyaada spread-out shape jo poorly shielded hai aur nucleus ko kam feel karta hai, toh uski energy ऊpar chali jaati hai.
Ek single shell ke andar, ek s electron nucleus ke sabse paas penetrate karta hai aur sabse tightly held hota hai, phir p, phir d, phir f.
Toh electron jo effective nuclear charge feel karta hai wo azimuthal number badhne ke saath ghatta hai, aur bilkul yahi ek shell ko alag energy levels mein split karta hai.
Ek saawdhaani: one-electron species ke liye aisा koi splitting नहीं $-$ energy sirf n par depend karti hai. Rule apply karne se pehle hamesha jaano ki aap kis regime mein ho.

sections.title: Writing configurations: anomalies and ions

board_events.text: Configurations, Cr/Cu anomalies, and cations
Find $Z$, then fill in $(n+l)$ order: 1s 2s 2p 3s 3p 4s 3d 4p 5s 4d 5p 6s ...
Capacities: $s$ holds 2, $p$ holds 6, $d$ holds 10, $f$ holds 14; apply Hund within a subshell.
Half-filled ($d^5$) and fully-filled ($d^{10}$) are extra stable: Cr $=$ [Ar]$3d^5 4s^1$, Cu $=$ [Ar]$3d^{10} 4s^1$.
For ions, remove electrons from the highest $n$ FIRST.
So 4s leaves before 3d, even though 4s filled first.
Never write Fe$^{2+}$ as [Ar]$3d^4 4s^2$ $-$ that is the classic error.

segments.text: Now we put the rules to work and write actual configurations, including the two famous exceptions.
Start by finding the number of electrons, then fill the subshells in n-plus-l order: one-s, two-s, two-p, three-s, three-p, four-s, three-d, four-p, and onward.
Respect the capacities as you go: s holds two, p holds six, d holds ten, f holds fourteen, and within any subshell you apply Hund's rule.
Now the exceptions. Half-filled and fully-filled d subshells carry extra exchange stability, so chromium is argon three-d-five four-s-one, and copper is argon three-d-ten four-s-one.
For ions there is one golden rule: remove electrons from the highest principal quantum number first.
Take iron, argon three-d-six four-s-two. To make iron two-plus, you strip the two four-s electrons, leaving argon three-d-six.
So the four-s electrons leave before the three-d electrons, even though four-s was filled first $-$ last in, but not last out.
Never write iron two-plus as argon three-d-four four-s-two. Removing three-d before four-s is the single most classic error in this topic.
Ab hum rules ko kaam par lagate hain aur asli configurations likhte hain, un do famous exceptions ke saath.
Electrons ki sankhya nikaalkar shuru karo, phir subshells ko n-plus-l order mein bharo: one-s, two-s, two-p, three-s, three-p, four-s, three-d, four-p, aur aage.
Chalte-chalte capacities ka dhyaan rakho: s holds two, p holds six, d holds ten, f holds fourteen, aur kisi bhi subshell ke andar aap Hund ka rule apply karte ho.
Ab exceptions. Half-filled aur fully-filled d subshells extra exchange stability rakhte hain, toh chromium argon three-d-five four-s-one hai, aur copper argon three-d-ten four-s-one.
Ions ke liye ek golden rule hai: electrons highest principal quantum number se pehle hataao.
Iron lo, argon three-d-six four-s-two. Iron two-plus banane ke liye, aap do four-s electrons strip karte ho, argon three-d-six chhodkar.
Toh four-s electrons three-d electrons se pehle jaate hain, chahe four-s pehle bharа tha $-$ last in, par last out नहीं.
Iron two-plus ko kabhi argon three-d-four four-s-two mat likho. Four-s se pehle three-d hataana is topic ki sabse classic galti hai.

An $s$ orbital is spherical: 1s has no node; 2s has one spherical (radial) node.
A $p$ orbital is a dumbbell with one nodal plane $-$ for $p_y$ that plane is the $xz$-plane.

board_events.text: A $d$ orbital has five members: four cloverleaf shapes with two nodal planes, plus $d_{z^2}$ with a ring.
Angular nodes ($=l$) carve the shape; radial nodes ($=n-l-1$) are nested spherical shells.

segments.text: Shape questions are exam staples, so let us fix the boundary-surface picture precisely and connect it to nodes.
An s orbital is spherical. A one-s has no node at all; a two-s has one spherical, radial node $-$ a thin shell inside which the probability briefly drops to zero.
A p orbital is a dumbbell with exactly one nodal plane, the plane perpendicular to its axis through the nucleus. For the p-y orbital that plane is the x-z plane.
Look at the two kinds of node: the flat plane that separates a dumbbell's lobes, and the spherical shell nested inside a larger orbital.
A d orbital has five members: four cloverleaf shapes each with two nodal planes, plus the odd one out, d-z-squared, with two lobes and a doughnut-shaped ring.
Keep the roles straight: angular nodes, equal to l, carve out the shape, while radial nodes, n minus l minus one, are the nested spherical shells.
There is a neat consequence for angular momentum: it equals the square root of l times l plus one, times h over two pi $-$ which is exactly zero for any s orbital.
And the nodes always total n minus one, so a higher shell, with more nodes, spreads the electron cloud over a larger, more structured region.
Shape ke sawaal exam staples hain, toh chalo boundary-surface picture ko precisely fix karein aur use nodes se joड़ein.
Ek s orbital spherical hai. Ek one-s ka koi node hi नहीं; ek two-s ka ek spherical, radial node hai $-$ ek patli shell jiske andar probability thoड़ी der ke liye zero ho jaati hai.
Ek p orbital ek dumbbell hai jismein theek ek nodal plane hai, wo plane jo iske axis ke perpendicular nucleus se guzarta hai. P-y orbital ke liye wo plane x-z plane hai.
Do kism ke node dekho: wo flat plane jo dumbbell ke lobes ko alag karta hai, aur wo spherical shell jo ek bade orbital ke andar nested hai.
Ek d orbital ke paanch members hain: chaar cloverleaf shapes har ek ke do nodal planes ke saath, plus wo alag wala, d-z-squared, do lobes aur ek doughnut-jaisी ring ke saath.
Roles seedhe rakho: angular nodes, l ke barabar, shape ko carve karte hain, jabki radial nodes, n minus l minus one, wo nested spherical shells hain.
Angular momentum ke liye ek neat consequence hai: ye barabar square root of l times l plus one, times h over two pi $-$ jo kisi bhi s orbital ke liye bilkul zero hai.
Aur nodes hamesha total n minus one hote hain, toh ek higher shell, zyaada nodes ke saath, electron cloud ko ek bade, zyaada structured region par phailaati hai.

sections.title: Quantum numbers and counting relations

board_events.text: Quantum numbers and counting relations
$n = 1,2,3,\dots$ (shell); $l = 0\dots(n-1)$ (shape, $s\,p\,d\,f$); $m_l = -l\dots+l$; $m_s = \pm\tfrac{1}{2}$.

board_events.latex: \text{orbitals in a subshell} = 2l+1, \quad \text{orbitals in a shell} = n^2

board_events.text: An $s$-electron ($l=0$) has zero orbital angular momentum.
Subshell capacities follow: $s$ 2, $p$ 6, $d$ 10, $f$ 14.
These counting relations are the backbone of every configuration question.

segments.text: Here is the compact reference for quantum numbers and the counting relations you will use on every configuration problem.

The principal number runs one, two, three, and up; the azimuthal runs from zero to n minus one, giving the s, p, d, f shapes; the magnetic runs minus l to plus l; and the spin is plus or minus one-half.
Orbital angular momentum is the square root of l times l plus one, times h over two pi, which we also write with h-bar.
For counting orbitals: a subshell holds two-l-plus-one orbitals, and a whole shell holds n-squared orbitals.
For counting electrons: a subshell holds at most four-l-plus-two, and a whole shell holds two-n-squared.
One immediate consequence: an s electron, with l zero, has exactly zero orbital angular momentum.
From the subshell formula, the familiar capacities follow directly: s takes two, p takes six, d takes ten, and f takes fourteen.
These counting relations are the backbone of every configuration and quantum-number question in the chapter $-$ commit them fully to memory.
Ye rahा quantum numbers aur un counting relations ka compact reference jo aap har configuration problem par use karoge.
Principal number one, two, three, aur ऊpar chalta hai; azimuthal zero se n minus one tak, s, p, d, f shapes deta hai; magnetic minus l se plus l; aur spin plus ya minus one-half.
Orbital angular momentum square root of l times l plus one, times h over two pi hai, jise hum h-bar se bhi likhte hain.
Orbitals ginne ke liye: ek subshell two-l-plus-one orbitals rakhti hai, aur ek poori shell n-squared orbitals.
Electrons ginne ke liye: ek subshell zyaada se zyaada four-l-plus-two rakhti hai, aur ek poori shell two-n-squared.
Ek turant consequence: ek s electron, l zero ke saath, ka orbital angular momentum bilkul zero hai.
Subshell formula se, jaani-pehchaani capacities seedhe nikalti hain: s two leta hai, p six, d ten, aur f fourteen.
Ye counting relations chapter ke har configuration aur quantum-number sawaal ki reeढ़ hain $-$ inhe poori tarah yaad kar lo.

sections.title: Nodes, the (n+l) rule, and the three principles

board_events.text: Nodes, energy order, and the three rules
$(n+l)$ rule: lower $(n+l)$ fills first; ties broken by lower $n$.
Aufbau: lowest energy first. Pauli: no two electrons share all four numbers. Hund: singly fill degenerate orbitals first.
One-electron species: energy depends on $n$ alone (2s and 2p degenerate).
Ions: remove the highest-$n$ electrons first (4s before 3d).

segments.text: The second reference card gathers nodes, the energy-ordering rule, and the three filling principles in one place.
Nodes first: radial nodes are n minus l minus one, angular nodes equal l, and the total is n minus one.
The energy-ordering rule is the n-plus-l rule: the subshell with the lower n-plus-l fills first, and ties are broken in favour of the lower n.
That produces the standard Aufbau order: one-s, two-s, two-p, three-s, three-p, four-s, three-d, four-p, five-s, and so on.
The three principles in one breath: Aufbau fills lowest energy first, Pauli forbids two electrons sharing all four numbers, and Hund fills degenerate orbitals singly before pairing.
Remember the special regime: for a one-electron species, energy depends on n alone, so two-s and two-p are degenerate, equal in energy.
Keep the two anomalies at your fingertips: chromium is argon three-d-five four-s-one, and copper is argon three-d-ten four-s-one.
And for ions, always strip the highest-n electrons first $-$ four-s leaves before three-d.
Doosra reference card nodes, energy-ordering rule, aur teen filling principles ko ek jagah ikattha karta hai.
Pehle nodes: radial nodes n minus l minus one, angular nodes barabar l, aur total n minus one.
Energy-ordering rule n-plus-l rule hai: jiska n-plus-l kam ho wo subshell pehle bharti hai, aur ties kam n ke haq mein toड़e jaate hain.
Wo standard Aufbau order banata hai: one-s, two-s, two-p, three-s, three-p, four-s, three-d, four-p, five-s, aur aage.

Teen principles ek saans mein: Aufbau lowest energy pehle bharta hai, Pauli do electrons ko saare chaar numbers share karne se rokta hai, aur Hund pairing se pehle degenerate orbitals ko singly bharta hai.
Special regime yaad rakho: one-electron species ke liye, energy sirf n par depend karti hai, toh two-s aur two-p degenerate hain, energy mein barabar.
Do anomalies ungliyon par rakho: chromium argon three-d-five four-s-one, aur copper argon three-d-ten four-s-one.
Aur ions ke liye, hamesha highest-n electrons pehle strip karo $-$ four-s three-d se pehle jaata hai.

sections.title: Worked example (CBSE): scandium configuration and quantum numbers

board_events.text: [CBSE] Scandium ($Z=21$): configuration and QN
The differentiating (last-filled) electron is the single 3d electron.
For a 3d electron: $n=3$; $l=2$ (the $d$ subshell).
Differentiating electron: $(n,l,m_l,m_s) = (3,\,2,\,-2,\,+\tfrac{1}{2})$.
Assign $m_l$ from the most negative value up, and spin $+\tfrac{1}{2}$ to the first occupant.

segments.text: Let us open the quantum-model worked examples with a standard board question on scandium.
Scandium has atomic number twenty-one, so we fill twenty-one electrons in n-plus-l order: one-s two, two-s two, two-p six, three-s two, three-p six, four-s two, and finally three-d one.
Written compactly, scandium is argon core, then three-d one, four-s two.
The differentiating electron $-$ the last one to enter $-$ is that single three-d electron, and we must give its four quantum numbers.
For a three-d electron the principal number is three, and the azimuthal number is two because it is in the d subshell.
By the standard filling convention, the first electron enters the most negative orbital, so the magnetic number is minus two, and being the first occupant its spin is plus one-half.
So the differentiating electron carries the set: n three, l two, magnetic minus two, spin plus one-half.
The routine is fixed: assign the magnetic number from the most negative value upward, and give plus one-half to the first electron in an orbital.
Quantum-model worked examples ko scandium par ek standard board sawaal se kholte hain.

Scandium ka atomic number twenty-one hai, toh hum ikkis electrons ko n-plus-l order mein bharte hain: one-s two, two-s two, two-p six, three-s two, three-p six, four-s two, aur aakhir mein three-d one.
Compactly likha, scandium argon core, phir three-d one, four-s two hai.
Differentiating electron $-$ jo aakhir mein aaya $-$ wahi single three-d electron hai, aur humein iske chaar quantum numbers dene hain.
Ek three-d electron ke liye principal number three hai, aur azimuthal number two kyunki wo d subshell mein hai.
Standard filling convention se, pehla electron sabse negative orbital mein jaata hai, toh magnetic number minus two hai, aur pehla occupant hone ke naate iska spin plus one-half.
Toh differentiating electron ka set hai: n three, l two, magnetic minus two, spin plus one-half.
Routine fixed hai: magnetic number sabse negative value se upar ki taraf assign karo, aur orbital ke pehle electron ko plus one-half do.

sections.title: Worked example (NEET): nodes of a 4d orbital

board_events.text: [NEET] Radial, angular, and total nodes of 4d
The trap: reporting $n-1$ as the radial count.
Self-check: radial $+$ angular $= 1 + 2 = 3 = n-1$.
Answer: one radial node, two angular nodes, three total.
If radial and angular do not sum to $n-1$, you have slipped somewhere.

segments.text: This is a quick node-counting question, and the whole risk is mixing up the three counts.
We want the radial, angular, and total nodes of a four-d orbital, where the principal number is four and the azimuthal number is two.
The classic trap is to report n minus one, which is three, as the radial count. That is the total, not the radial.
The radial count is n minus l minus one, which is four minus two minus one, giving one radial node.
The angular count is simply l, which is two, and the total is n minus one, which is three.
Now the self-check that saves you: radial plus angular is one plus two, which equals three, the value of n minus one. Everything is consistent.
So the answer is one radial node, two angular nodes, and three total nodes.
Carry the habit forward: if your radial and angular counts do not add up to n minus one, you have slipped somewhere and should recheck.
Ye ek quick node-counting sawaal hai, aur poora khatra teen counts ko mix karne mein hai.
Humein ek four-d orbital ke radial, angular aur total nodes chahiye, jahaan principal number four hai aur azimuthal number two.
Classic trap hai n minus one, jo three hai, ko radial count report karna. Wo total hai, radial नहीं.
Radial count n minus l minus one hai, jo four minus two minus one, ek radial node deta hai.
Angular count bas l hai, jo two hai, aur total n minus one hai, jo three hai.
Ab wo self-check jo aapko bachaata hai: radial plus angular one plus two hai, jo three ke barabar, n minus one ka value. Sab consistent hai.
Toh jawaab hai ek radial node, do angular nodes, aur teen total nodes.
Aadat aage le jao: agar aapke radial aur angular counts n minus one mein add नहीं hote, toh aap kahin phisle ho aur dobara check karna chahiye.

sections.title: Worked example (JEE Main): 3d subshell and Fe2+

board_events.text: [JEE Main] 3d subshell facts and Fe$^{2+}$
Neutral iron is [Ar] 3d$^6$ 4s$^2$.
Remove the two highest-$n$ electrons first $-$ the 4s pair.
The 4s electrons leave before the 3d, even though 4s filled first.

segments.text: This J E E Main example stacks several small facts about the three-d subshell and finishes with an ion configuration.
First, the orbital angular momentum of a three-d electron. With l equal to two, it is the square root of two times three, which is the square root of six, times h over two pi.
Second, the counting. The subshell has two-l-plus-one, that is five orbitals, and holds at most four-l-plus-two, that is ten electrons.
Third, the radial nodes of a three-d orbital: n minus l minus one is three minus two minus one, which is zero $-$ a three-d orbital has no radial node.
Now the configuration. Neutral iron is argon core, three-d six, four-s two.
To form iron two-plus, remove the two highest-principal-number electrons first, which is the four-s pair.
That leaves iron two-plus as argon core, three-d six $-$ clean and complete.
Note the catch that trips everyone: the four-s electrons leave before the three-d, even though four-s was filled first.
Ye J E E Main example three-d subshell ke kai chhote facts ko stack karta hai aur ek ion configuration par khatam hota hai.
Pehle, ek three-d electron ka orbital angular momentum. l barabar two ke saath, ye square root of two times three, yaani square root of six, times h over two pi hai.
Doosra, counting. Subshell ke paas two-l-plus-one, yaani paanch orbitals hain, aur ye zyaada se zyaada four-l-plus-two, yaani das electrons rakhti hai.
Teesra, ek three-d orbital ke radial nodes: n minus l minus one barabar three minus two minus one, jo zero hai $-$ ek three-d orbital ka koi radial node नहीं.
Ab configuration. Neutral iron argon core, three-d six, four-s two hai.
Iron two-plus banane ke liye, do highest-principal-number electrons pehle hataao, jo four-s pair hai.
Wo iron two-plus ko argon core, three-d six chhodta hai $-$ clean aur complete.
Wo catch note karo jo sabko phasaata hai: four-s electrons three-d se pehle jaate hain, chahe four-s pehle bharа tha.

sections.title: Worked example (JEE Advanced): a universe with three spin values

board_events.text: [JEE Advanced] Three spin values change the capacities
Suppose spin takes three values ($-\tfrac{1}{2}, 0, +\tfrac{1}{2}$); all other rules unchanged. Find the $n=3$ capacity and the $Z=10$ configuration.
Orbital counts come from $n$ and $l$, NOT spin $-$ so they are unchanged.
New subshell capacities: $s$ holds 3, $p$ holds 9, $d$ holds 15.
Electron capacity $=$ (orbital count) $\times$ (number of spin values) $-$ the whole trick.

segments.text: This is a genuine J E E Advanced favourite: change one rule of the universe and test whether you understand where each count comes from.

Suppose the spin quantum number could take three values $-$ minus one-half, zero, and plus one-half $-$ while every other rule stays the same. We want the new capacity of the third shell and the configuration for atomic number ten.
The crucial realisation is that orbital counts come only from n and l, not from spin, so the number of orbitals is completely unchanged.
The third shell still has n-squared, that is nine orbitals.
But each orbital can now hold three electrons, one per spin value, so the shell's capacity is three times nine, which is twenty-seven electrons.
The subshell capacities scale the same way: s now holds three, p holds three times three which is nine, and d holds three times five which is fifteen.
Now seat ten electrons in n-plus-l order. One-s takes three, two-s takes three, and the remaining four go into two-p, which can hold up to nine.
So the atom with atomic number ten is one-s three, two-s three, two-p four. The whole trick is that electron capacity equals orbital count times the number of spin values.
Ye ek asli J E E Advanced favourite hai: universe ka ek rule badlo aur test karo ki aap samajhte ho ki har count aata kahaan se hai.

Maano spin quantum number teen values le sakta $-$ minus one-half, zero, aur plus one-half $-$ jabki har doosra rule same rehta hai. Humein teesri shell ki nayi capacity aur atomic number ten ki configuration chahiye.
Crucial realisation ye hai ki orbital counts sirf n aur l se aate hain, spin se नहीं, toh orbitals ki sankhya bilkul unchanged hai.
Teesri shell mein ab bhi n-squared, yaani nau orbitals hain.
Par har orbital ab teen electrons rakh sakta hai, ek per spin value, toh shell ki capacity three times nine, jo twenty-seven electrons hai.
Subshell capacities ussi tarah scale hoti hain: s ab three rakhta hai, p three times three yaani nau, aur d three times five yaani pandrah.
Ab das electrons ko n-plus-l order mein bithao. One-s teen leta hai, two-s teen leta hai, aur bache chaar two-p mein jaate hain, jo nau tak rakh sakta hai.
Toh atomic number ten wala atom one-s three, two-s three, two-p four hai. Poora trick ye hai ki electron capacity barabar orbital count times spin values ki sankhya.

board_events.text: Quantum-number traps
Pitfall 1: confusing node types $-$ radial $= n-l-1$, angular $= l$, total $= n-1$.
Pitfall 2: assuming lower $n$ means lower energy $-$ in multi-electron atoms the $(n+l)$ rule rules.
Pitfall 3: removing 3d before 4s for cations $-$ electrons leave the highest $n$ first.
Pitfall 4: forgetting the Cr and Cu anomalies $-$ half- and fully-filled subshells steal a 4s electron.
For 'is this set of quantum numbers allowed?', check the chain: $l \lt n$ and $|m_l| \le l$. One violation means impossible.
Pro-tip: for ions, write the neutral atom first, then strip the highest-$n$ electrons.
For node counts, anchor on total $= n-1$ and split it into radial and angular.

segments.text: Let us close the densest subtopic of the chapter with its four recurring traps and two quick pro-tips.
The first trap is confusing node types. Fix them once: radial is n minus l minus one, angular is l, and total is n minus one.
The second is assuming lower n always means lower energy. In multi-electron atoms it is the n-plus-l rule that rules, which is why four-s fills before three-d.
The third is removing three-d before four-s when forming cations. Electrons always leave from the highest principal number first, so four-s goes before three-d.
The fourth is forgetting the chromium and copper anomalies. Half-filled and fully-filled d subshells steal a four-s electron for extra stability.

For any question asking whether a set of quantum numbers is allowed, check the chain instantly: l must be less than n, and the size of the magnetic number must not exceed l. One violation makes it impossible.
<whisper>Here is the pro-tip for ions: always write the neutral atom first, then strip the highest-n electrons. It prevents the classic three-d-before-four-s error every time.</whisper>
And for node counts, anchor on the total being n minus one, then split it into radial and angular. That anchor catches almost every slip.
Chalo chapter ke sabse dense subtopic ko iske chaar recurring traps aur do quick pro-tips ke saath band karein.
Pehla trap node types ko confuse karna hai. Inhe ek baar fix karo: radial n minus l minus one, angular l, aur total n minus one.
Doosra ye maanna hai ki kam n hamesha kam energy ka matlab hai. Multi-electron atoms mein n-plus-l rule raaj karta hai, isiliye four-s three-d se pehle bharta hai.
Teesra cations banate waqt three-d ko four-s se pehle hataana hai. Electrons hamesha highest principal number se pehle jaate hain, toh four-s three-d se pehle jaata hai.
Chautha chromium aur copper ke anomalies bhoolna hai. Half-filled aur fully-filled d subshells extra stability ke liye ek four-s electron chura lete hain.

Kisi bhi sawaal ke liye jo poochta hai ki quantum numbers ka set allowed hai ya नहीं, chain turant check karo: l ko n se kam hona chahiye, aur magnetic number ka size l se zyaada नहीं hona chahiye. Ek violation ise impossible bana deta hai.
<whisper>Ye rahा ions ke liye pro-tip: hamesha pehle neutral atom likho, phir highest-n electrons strip karo. Ye classic three-d-before-four-s galti har baar rokta hai.</whisper>
Aur node counts ke liye, total ko n minus one par anchor karo, phir use radial aur angular mein split karo. Wo anchor lagbhag har slip pakad leta hai.
